generation.hypothesis: Using in-situ high-temperature characterization (e.g., synchrotron-based high-temperature X-ray diffraction) to monitor the formation of protective oxide layers on silicide-coated high-temperature alloys can enable real-time optimization of the coating process, thereby enhancing oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Metal or alloy substrates that are prone to oxidation at high temperatures (for example, refractory high-entropy alloys or MoNbTaTiW alloys) in their unprotected state.
generation.intervention: Apply a silicide coating (such as a Si-20Cr-20Fe coating) and implement in-situ synchrotron-based high-temperature XRD during oxidation to dynamically observe and adjust protective scale formation.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidative environments representative of service conditions (e.g., temperatures above 1000°C) where oxidation kinetics critically affect material performance.
generation.structural_mediator: Development of a dense, adherent protective oxide or silicide scale that forms by transformation of the initial coating layer.
generation.mechanism: The in-situ XRD method provides real-time feedback on phase evolution and kinetics of protective layer formation, allowing adjustments in processing parameters to optimize the structure and composition of the scale, which in turn impedes further oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced oxidation resistance through the formation of a more effective protective layer; the dynamic monitoring should allow fine-tuning of the coating process, leading to improved scale density and adhesion compared to standard treatments without real-time characterization.
generation.baseline: Coated alloys processed using conventional methods without in-situ monitoring, where protective layer formation is only characterized post-treatment.
generation.boundary: This approach is specifically applicable to high-temperature oxidation conditions. Its effectiveness outside these conditions (e.g., at lower temperatures or over extremely long exposure times) remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance is uncertain until experimental calibration is done. Additionally, the method's sensitivity and suitability across a wide range of alloy types require further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical high-temperature alloy samples with a Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating. Subject one set to high-temperature oxidation while performing in-situ synchrotron-based XRD to monitor phase evolution. Process a control set using conventional post-mortem characterization after oxidation. Compare both sets regarding oxide layer structure, thickness, and mass gain.
measurements: Real-time XRD patterns to track phase transitions and kinetics under oxidation conditions
Electron microscopy to measure the protective layer thickness and assess microstructural integrity
Thermogravimetric analysis to monitor mass gain as a function of oxidation time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in-situ monitoring does not provide actionable data that leads to discernable improvements in the microstructure (e.g., denser or more adherent oxide layers) or the oxidation resistance (e.g., reduced mass gain) compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. decision.trend: Earlier studies aimed at improving oxidation resistance have predominantly relied on surface treatments that form protective coatings. For example, the work using a Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating on MoNbTaTiW alloys demonstrated that a two-layer silicide structure could evolve into a protective oxide scale during high‐temperature exposure. Parallel studies have detailed oxidation mechanisms via in‐situ high‐temperature characterizations, revealing the formation, thickness, and phase evolution of oxide layers. Although these approaches have successfully improved oxidation resistance by promoting the formation of a dense barrier, they typically do not provide real‐time feedback on the kinetics of protective layer formation under service conditions.
decision.unsolved: What remains unsolved is the lack of a method that can dynamically measure and optimize the formation of the protective oxide or silicide layers at operating temperatures. Without real‐time monitoring, it is difficult to tune processing parameters for achieving the most effective, adherent, and protective scale.
decision.lever: in-situ high-temperature characterization (e.g., synchrotron-based high-temperature X-ray diffraction)
decision.why: This approach follows naturally from the trend because previous research established that a silicide coating can form a protective oxide layer, but the kinetics of that transformation under actual service conditions still remain imprecise. A real-time in-situ measurement method will provide the necessary feedback to optimize coating composition and processing parameters, thereby directly addressing the current gap in understanding and control of oxidation-resistance mechanisms.
